title: Physics-Guided Flow-Map Matchingfor Precipitation Nowcasting

paper.title: Physics-Guided Flow-Map Matching for Precipitation Nowcasting
paper.abstract:
Abstract Precipitation nowcasting, generating future radar fields from past
observations, is critical for flood warning and disaster response. It is
also a demanding benchmark for spatiotemporal generative modeling, with
chaotic dynamics, heavy-tailed intensities, and rare high-intensity
structures that matter most. Deterministic models
minimize a pixel loss and are driven toward the conditional mean, which blurs
exactly those structures, while generative models that add a stochastic
residual on top of a deterministic backbone inherit the same blur.
We propose Physics-Guided Flow-Map Matching (PG-FMM), a conditional flow-map
model that decouples predictable advection from uncertain small-scale detail. A
frozen Lagrangian advection prior transports the radar field and supplies an
explicit motion forecast, and a flow-map generative head, conditioned on
the past frames and the prior rollout rather than summed onto it, produces
sharp stochastic detail in four sampling steps. The prior serves only as
guidance, so the head replaces blurred structure instead of inheriting it.
Extensive experiments on four radar benchmarks show that PG-FMM outperforms
state-of-the-art methods on 18 18 of 24 24 metrics, with the largest gains at
heavy-rain thresholds, where the critical success index improves by up to 58.9 % 58.9\% .
The project page can be found at https://neurogica.github.io/PG-FMM .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : Three families of precipitation nowcasters: (1) deterministic models blur high-intensity cells; (2) purely generative models can drift off the observed storm track; (3) our physics-guided design conditions a flow-map head on a frozen advection prior, keeping forecasts sharp and on track. Precipitation nowcasting generates the next one to two hours of high-resolution reflectivity fields from a short history of radar frames. It is conditional video prediction in a demanding regime, as the dynamics are chaotic, the intensity distribution is heavy-tailed, and forecast value is concentrated in rare high-intensity structures. Nowcasts underpin flood early warning, disaster response, water management, and the safe operation of transport and energy infrastructure [ 2 , 43 , 60 ] , and their importance grows as a warming climate intensifies short-duration convective rainfall extremes and the flash flooding they cause [ 12 ] ; the short lead time of a nowcast often separates an effective response from a costly one. A useful nowcast must therefore forecast where and how strongly convective cells will develop, not merely whether it will rain. This high-intensity regime is also the hardest, because small-scale convective growth and decay are only partly predictable. Deterministic video predictors minimize a per-pixel regression loss and are therefore driven toward the conditional mean of the future, so their forecasts blur [ 46 , 47 , 54 , 14 , 16 ] . The blur erases sharp, high-intensity cores, and detection skill at the heaviest thresholds decays toward zero as the lead time grows. This failure mode is shared even by strong recent predictors such as PhyDNet [ 26 ] and AlphaPre [ 28 ] , because a mean-seeking objective smooths extremes regardless of the backbone. A faithful nowcaster must therefore be generative, sampling sharp and plausible fields rather than averaging them. Existing generative nowcasters address sharpness but leave two gaps. Many recent diffusion-based methods anchor the forecast on a deterministic backbone, refining it or adding a stochastic residual to it [ 18 , 59 ] ; because that backbone is trained with a pixel loss, it carries conditional-mean blur, which the anchored forecast inherits at long lead times. Purely generative models, including GAN- and flow-based nowcasters [ 43 , 39 ] , avoid the anchor but discard the predictable part of the dynamics, namely the advective motion that a simple physical model already captures well, and must relearn it from data, which can drift the forecast off the observed storm track. These gaps motivate a design that retains the motion skill of a physical model while letting a generative model render the unpredictable detail, without either contaminating the other. Figure 1 contrasts deterministic, purely generative, and our physics-guided designs. In this paper we propose Physics-Guided Flow-Map Matching (PG-FMM), a generative nowcaster that guides a flow-map generative head with a frozen physical motion model. A lightweight Lagrangian advection prior is pre-trained once and then frozen; it rolls the observed field forward through a learned velocity and source term and supplies an explicit motion forecast. A flow-map generative head then produces the future sequence conditioned on both the history and this prior rollout. A central design choice is that the prior enters as a conditioning signal rather than as an additive residual, so the head can replace the prior’s blurred structure with sharper detail while still exploiting its motion skill, and the physical rollout keeps the convection on a plausible trajectory. Here physics-guided means that the prior’s rollout is a discretized advection equation in which only the coefficient fields are learned ( Sec. 4.2 ). Casting the generator as a two-time flow map rather than an instantaneous velocity field lets it produce a forecast in a few network evaluations, in line with recent flow-map and consistency models [ 6 , 48 ] . This separation of predictable motion from stochastic detail follows the decoupling logic proposed in [ 34 ] . Across four standard radar benchmarks and six metrics each, PG-FMM outperforms the state-of-the-art AlphaPre [ 28 ] on 18 18 of the 24 24 metrics, and the margins are largest precisely at the heavy-rain thresholds where mean-seeking methods fail. Code and pretrained checkpoints are publicly available. 1 1 1 https://github.com/Neurogica/PG-FMM The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. ∙ \bullet We propose PG-FMM, which guides a generative flow-map head with a frozen Lagrangian advection prior used as conditioning rather than an additive residual, so conditional-mean blur is never inherited additively. ∙ \bullet We introduce, to our knowledge, the first flow-map-matching formulation for precipitation nowcasting, coupling a learned semi-Lagrangian advection prior with a two-time transport head whose few-step sampling makes the inference-time ensemble affordable. ∙ \bullet We show on the SEVIR, MeteoNet, Shanghai, and CIKM benchmarks that PG-FMM surpasses AlphaPre on 18 18 of 24 24 metrics, with the largest gains at the heavy-rain thresholds, and we isolate the prior’s contribution with controlled ablations, which show that its benefit stems from the physics content rather than from conditioning alone.

sections.heading: 2.1 Video Prediction and Precipitation Nowcasting
sections.text: Radar nowcasting is a conditional video-prediction problem, and the two literatures have co-evolved since ConvLSTM [ 46 ] , which was introduced for nowcasting and became a standard video-prediction baseline [ 36 , 33 ] . Deterministic sequence predictors developed on video transfer directly to radar, including trajectory-aware recurrence (TrajGRU [ 47 ] , the PredRNN family [ 54 , 53 , 55 ] , MotionRNN [ 56 ] ), efficient convolutional designs (SimVP [ 14 ] , MAU [ 8 ] ), and transformer and operator backbones (Earthformer [ 16 ] , Rainformer [ 4 ] ); physically structured predictors such as PhyDNet [ 26 ] and the recent amplitude–phase model AlphaPre [ 28 ] , the strongest deterministic predictor on the benchmarks we use, continue this line, and surveys cover both the video and the weather perspective [ 2 , 45 ] . Because a squared- or absolute-error objective is minimized by the conditional mean, all of these models tend to blur, and the blur is most damaging at high reflectivity where sharp convective cells are smoothed away. Stochastic video generation addresses the blur by sampling futures rather than averaging them, as in video-diffusion predictors such as MCVD [ 52 ] and STRPM [ 7 ] . On radar, DGMR [ 43 ] uses a conditional GAN, and NowcastNet [ 60 ] couples a deterministic evolution operator with a generative network. Diffusion and latent-diffusion models have since become dominant. PreDiff [ 15 ] and LDCast [ 27 ] perform latent diffusion, CasCast [ 18 ] cascades a deterministic prediction with a latent diffusion refiner, and DiffCast [ 59 ] adds a stochastic residual on top of an arbitrary deterministic backbone. We refer to the latter recipe as a residual anchor: the forecast is a deterministic prediction plus a generated residual. Because the deterministic part is trained with a pixel loss, it carries conditional-mean blur that the sum cannot remove, particularly at long lead times. Diffusion models for the broader weather-forecasting problem [ 40 , 50 , 35 ] share the same generative motivation at coarser scales.

sections.heading: 2.2 Flow Matching and Flow Maps
sections.text: Continuous-time generative models have matured rapidly, and recent surveys [ 58 , 30 ] cover the progression from score-based diffusion [ 19 , 49 , 21 ] to simulation-free transport. Flow Matching [ 29 ] , Rectified Flow [ 32 ] , and Stochastic Interpolants [ 1 ] regress an instantaneous velocity field whose probability-flow ODE must be integrated with many steps at sampling time. Flow-Map Matching [ 6 ] instead learns the finite-time flow map (the two-time transport operator), so that a sample is produced in a few network evaluations, or even one; Consistency Models [ 48 ] , Consistency Trajectory Models [ 22 ] , and Shortcut Models [ 13 ] reach the same few-step regime through self-consistency, trajectory matching, and step-size conditioning, and distillation offers a complementary route [ 44 ] ; data-to-data diffusion bridges [ 31 , 61 ] are related transport formulations. In nowcasting, FlowCast [ 39 ] applies conditional flow matching in a latent space. We adopt a flow-map head because its few-step sampling makes a multi-member inference ensemble affordable, which is otherwise prohibitive for long diffusion chains.

sections.heading: 2.3 Physics-Informed and Lagrangian Forecasting
sections.text: Physics-informed machine learning injects physical knowledge into data-driven models through soft PDE-residual penalties, structured operators, or explicit dynamics, and is reviewed comprehensively by Karniadakis et al . [ 20 , 42 ] . In precipitation nowcasting, a long operational tradition extrapolates the radar field along estimated motion, as in the optical-flow libraries PySTEPS [ 41 ] and rainymotion [ 3 ] ; such Lagrangian advection is accurate for short horizons but cannot represent growth or decay. Learning-based work reintroduces the missing source term while keeping the motion explicit: NowcastNet [ 60 ] learns a neural evolution operator with an additive intensity update, PhyDNet [ 26 ] disentangles physical dynamics from residual factors in a latent space, and the differentiable Lagrangian network LUPIN [ 38 ] separates advection from an advection-free growth/decay branch. Beyond nowcasting, large data-driven weather models [ 37 , 5 , 24 , 23 ] extend physically informed architectures to global forecasting. Our prior follows the explicit warp-and-source route but keeps the physics module lightweight and, after a short pre-training stage, frozen, so that it supplies motion skill as a conditioning signal, not a constraint on the generative head.

sections.heading: 3.1 Problem Setting
sections.text: We address radar precipitation nowcasting. A model observes a history of T in T_{\mathrm{in}} past radar frames and predicts the next T out T_{\mathrm{out}} frames, where each frame is a single-channel reflectivity field R ∈ ℝ H × W R\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} on a spatial grid of size H × W H\times W normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . We write the observed history as R 1 : T in R_{1:T_{\mathrm{in}}} and the prediction target as x 0 = R T in + 1 : T in + T out ∈ ℝ T out × H × W , x_{0}=R_{T_{\mathrm{in}}+1:\,T_{\mathrm{in}}+T_{\mathrm{out}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{\mathrm{out}}\times H\times W}, (1) where the T out T_{\mathrm{out}} future frames are stacked along the channel axis for the convolutional networks. The horizon lengths T in , T out T_{\mathrm{in}},T_{\mathrm{out}} , the grid size H × W H\times W , and the per-dataset intensity scale used to recover physical units are dataset-specific and are listed in Sec. 5 . Because convective growth and decay are only partly determined by the recent past, the future is inherently uncertain. We therefore model the conditional distribution p ( x 0 ∣ R 1 : T in ) p(x_{0}\mid R_{1:T_{\mathrm{in}}}) and draw an ensemble of forecasts from it rather than predicting a single field. A useful forecast combines high detection skill at the operational intensity thresholds, especially the heavy-rain thresholds, with low pixel error and sharp structure. We report the Critical Success Index (CSI) per threshold and averaged, the Heidke Skill Score (HSS), SSIM, and MSE, with formal definitions deferred to Sec. 5 ; the primary metrics are the mean CSI and the high-threshold CSI.

sections.text: Figure 2 : Overview of PG-FMM. A frozen Lagrangian advection prior g ϕ g_{\phi} produces an explicit motion forecast, and a flow-map head f θ f_{\theta} , conditioned on the history and the prior rollout, maps noise to the future sequence in a few transport steps. sections.heading: 4.1 Overview
sections.text: PG-FMM forecasts precipitation by separating the predictable advective motion of the radar field from the uncertain small-scale detail, so that neither part contaminates the other. The model has two modules ( Fig. 2 ): a frozen Lagrangian advection prior g ϕ g_{\phi} ( Sec. 4.2 ) that turns the observed history into an explicit motion forecast, and a flow-map generative head f θ f_{\theta} ( Sec. 4.3 ) that, conditioned on the history and the prior rollout, samples the future sequence. At inference we aggregate a small ensemble with a probability-matched mean ( Sec. 4.4 ). The prior is used only as conditioning and is never added to the output, unlike residual-anchor nowcasters [ 18 , 59 ] , whose pixel-loss backbone carries its conditional-mean blur into the anchored forecast ( Sec. 2 ). Passing the physical forecast as a conditioning signal instead lets the generative head replace the prior’s blurred structure with sharp detail while still exploiting its motion skill. The decoupling does not depend on the particular modules, as any per-step motion model and any conditional generative head could be substituted. Ours pairs a learned warp-and-source prior with a flow-map head whose few-step sampling keeps the ensemble affordable.

sections.text: Because f θ f_{\theta} is a transport operator, a forecast is produced with a small number of function evaluations (NFE). On a decreasing time grid 1 = τ 0 > τ 1 > ⋯ > τ N = 0 1{=}\tau_{0}>\tau_{1}>\dots>\tau_{N}{=}0 , we initialize x τ 0 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{\tau_{0}}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and iterate as x τ i + 1 = f θ ( x τ i , c ; τ i , τ i + 1 ) , i = 0 , … , N − 1 , x_{\tau_{i+1}}=f_{\theta}\big(x_{\tau_{i}},c;\tau_{i},\tau_{i+1}\big),\qquad i=0,\dots,N-1, (9) returning clip [ 0 , 1 ] ⁡ ( x τ N ) \operatorname{clip}_{[0,1]}(x_{\tau_{N}}) , where N N is the number of sampling steps; each step is one evaluation of f θ f_{\theta} , so a forecast costs exactly N N NFE. We use exponential-moving-average weights of the trained network. A single draw is sharp, but its small-scale detail varies with the noise seed. Few-step sampling makes it inexpensive to draw an ensemble of K K independent samples from different noise seeds and combine them with a probability-matched mean (PMM) [ 11 ] . Averaging the members directly would blur again, since displaced peaks cancel; the PMM instead takes the spatial pattern of the ensemble mean, which places precipitation reliably, and remaps its values, rank by rank, onto the value distribution pooled over all K K members, so the high-amplitude peaks that plain averaging smooths away are restored, which is decisive for high-threshold CSI. We report the full PMM for verification metrics and, for qualitative figures, a single sample, which is visually sharper; the operating-point values N N and K K are given in Sec. 5 .

sections.heading: 5.1 Datasets and Protocol
sections.text: We evaluate on four standard radar benchmarks spanning different regions and sensors: SEVIR (United States; vertically integrated liquid, VIL) [ 51 ] , MeteoNet (France) [ 25 ] , Shanghai Radar (China) [ 9 ] , and CIKM [ 10 ] . Following the AlphaPre protocol [ 28 ] , every frame is resized to H × W = 128 × 128 H{\times}W{=}128{\times}128 and normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , and we predict T out T_{\mathrm{out}} future frames from T in = 5 T_{\mathrm{in}}{=}5 past frames, with T out = 20 T_{\mathrm{out}}{=}20 on SEVIR, MeteoNet and Shanghai and T out = 10 T_{\mathrm{out}}{=}10 on CIKM. We use each benchmark’s official splits throughout: SEVIR provides 12,182 12{,}182 training and 8,096 8{,}096 test sequences; MeteoNet 6,308 6{,}308 / 1,310 1{,}310 ; Shanghai 1,381 1{,}381 / 526 526 (a 10 % 10\% tail of the official 1,534 1{,}534 training sequences is held out for validation, with no test leakage); and CIKM 1,000 1{,}000 / 4,000 4{,}000 . Each dataset keeps its native intensity scale, thresholds and evaluator, so all numbers are comparable.

sections.heading: 5.2 Implementation Details
sections.text: The two modules are trained in sequence with AdamW (learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , batch size 8 8 ) and exponential-moving-average weights (decay 0.999 0.999 ). The Lagrangian prior is trained first and then frozen; the flow-map head is then trained for 297.6 297.6 k steps for the headline SEVIR model, and every ablation variant uses a matched 150 150 k-step budget. The prior U-Net uses base width 96 96 with channel multipliers ( 1 , 2 , 4 , 4 ) (1,2,4,4) ; the flow-map U-Net uses base width 128 128 with multipliers ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ) (1,2,3,4) and self-attention at the two coarsest scales. At inference we use N = 4 N{=}4 sampling steps and a K = 16 K{=}16 -member probability-matched-mean ensemble, i.e., 64 64 network evaluations per forecast ( 1.2 1.2 forecasts/s on one GPU; a single sample runs at 7.2 7.2 /s). Training and evaluation run on one NVIDIA GB202 GPU ( 96 96 GB), and checkpoints are selected by validation skill. Full hyperparameters, per-dataset training steps, and timing are listed in the supplementary material.

sections.heading: 5.5 Qualitative Results
sections.text: Figure 4 shows two cases over the full 100 100 -minute horizon (single samples, the sharper qualitative view; verification uses the probability-matched mean, Sec. 4.4 ). On the Nebraska convective system (top), PG-FMM preserves the sharp, high-intensity core at every lead time while AlphaPre progressively attenuates and blurs it; the frozen prior keeps the convection on its observed track while the generative head restores intensity. The same behavior holds on the remnants of Hurricane Barry (bottom). To test whether these examples are representative rather than favorable, we ranked all 2,672 2{,}672 heavy-rain SEVIR test samples (ground-truth max VIL ≥ 120 \geq 120 ) by the per-sample CSI-160 gain over AlphaPre at the reported operating point; AlphaPre attains the higher CSI-160 on 351 351 of them ( 13.1 % 13.1\% ). Figure 5 shows a representative failure, a convective system over north Texas where the generative head drops the heavy-rain band that both the ground truth and the deterministic baseline retain. The supplementary material provides additional cases on SEVIR and MeteoNet. sections.heading: 5.6 Ablation Study
sections.text: Four generative variants share an identical flow-map head, identical conditioning, and a matched 150 150 k-step training budget on SEVIR, and differ only in the content of the prior rollout ( Tab. 2 ): no prior, classical semi-Lagrangian advection driven by optical flow, a learned deterministic nowcaster (AlphaPre) used as the prior, and our frozen Lagrangian physics prior. The physics prior is best on every metric except SSIM, followed by the learned deterministic prior, and classical advection trails even the no-prior variant on every detection metric. The content of the prior is therefore what matters: a poor prior is worse than no prior at all, so the gains cannot be explained by conditioning alone. The one exception, SSIM, rewards smoother output, as the Prior only row below shows most clearly. The full model in Tab. 1 uses a longer schedule, hence its slightly higher numbers; per-lead-time curves in the supplementary material show that the physics prior’s margin emerges at long lead times. The generative head is likewise necessary. The frozen prior alone (Prior only in Tab. 2 ) is already a strong deterministic baseline, yet it trails the full model on every skill metric; its best-in-table SSIM reflects smoothness, and the head adds the sharpness and probabilistic skill (CRPS). Together, these ablations justify the motion–generative decoupling. The supplementary material reports further studies. Composition consistency ( Eq. 8 ) appears to improve fidelity and stability rather than detection skill, so we keep it enabled. An ensemble-size sweep supports the 16 16 -member operating point, and even a single draw ( K = 1 K{=}1 , CSI-M 0.3394 0.3394 ) at N = 4 N{=}4 network evaluations exceeds AlphaPre’s published CSI-M. A fusion ablation indicates that conditioning, unlike additive residual fusion, is robust to the quality of the prior. Structural metrics suggest that the heavy-rain gain reflects recovered heavy rain rather than inflated area, and a matched-ensemble comparison with a reproduced generative baseline indicates that the margin persists.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We addressed radar precipitation nowcasting in the high-intensity regime, where existing models blur the strongest convective cells. PG-FMM decouples predictable advection from uncertain small-scale detail and conditions a flow-map head on a frozen physical prior rather than summing a residual onto it, so no conditional-mean blur is additively inherited. Under a unified protocol over four radar benchmarks, PG-FMM surpassed the state-of-the-art AlphaPre on 18 18 of 24 24 metrics, with the largest margins at the heavy-rain thresholds where mean-seeking methods fail, and controlled ablations isolated the contributions of the prior and the head. Two limitations remain. The raw ensemble is under-dispersive, with a spread-to-RMSE ratio of about 0.43 0.43 and a U-shaped rank histogram (supplementary material). The probability-matched mean compensates for this only at the verification level, so probabilistic use beyond the reported CRPS and Brier scores requires explicit spread calibration. All results also come from single-seed training on 128 × 128 128{\times}128 rasters under one protocol with lead times up to 100 100 minutes, and, as with any advection-based nowcaster, PG-FMM under-forecasts initiation and re-intensification without precursors, can under-carry heavy bands ( Sec. 5 ) or over-persist dissipating storms (supplementary material). Addressing these limitations and extending the decoupling to other spatiotemporal tasks are natural next steps.

sections.heading: A Skill versus Lead Time for the Prior Ablation
sections.text: Figure 6 : Skill versus lead time for the prior ablation on SEVIR: CSI averaged over thresholds (a) and at the heavy-rain threshold VIL = 181 {=}181 (b). The margin of the physics prior emerges at long lead times and is largest on heavy rain. Figure 6 complements the prior ablation (Table 2 of the main paper) with per-lead-time detection skill. All four variants share an identical flow-map head, identical conditioning, and a matched training budget on SEVIR, and are evaluated at the unified operating point ( 16 16 -member probability-matched mean, four sampling steps); only the content of the prior rollout differs. Two observations mirror the aggregate table. First, the physics prior is indistinguishable from the alternatives at short lead times, where advection is easy, and its margin appears and grows at longer lead times, the regime where an informative motion prior matters. Second, the classical advection prior degrades fastest, falling below the no-prior variant, which indicates that a poor prior actively misleads the generative head and that the gains of our prior come from its content rather than from conditioning alone.

sections.heading: B Spread–Skill Diagnostic and Sampling-Seed Variability
sections.text: Figure 7 : Spread–skill diagnostic of PG-FMM on SEVIR: ensemble spread and ensemble-mean RMSE per lead time (normalized VIL units). The spread/RMSE ratio is stable at ≈ 0.43 {\approx}0.43 , indicating a sharp but under-dispersive ensemble. Figure 7 reports the spread–skill relation of the full model on the SEVIR test set, namely the ensemble spread (standard deviation across the 16 16 members) and the ensemble-mean RMSE per lead time, in normalized VIL units. The spread grows monotonically with lead time, as the ensemble widens when the forecast becomes less certain, and the spread-to-RMSE ratio is stable at ≈ 0.43 {\approx}0.43 . The ensemble is therefore under-dispersive, the common regime for radar nowcast ensembles, which trade calibration of the raw members for sharpness; this is consistent with the strong CRPS of the probability-matched mean. Improving member-level dispersion, for example through spread calibration or larger ensembles, is left as future work. Sampling-seed variability at the reported operating point, summarized in the main paper, is negligible. Across three independent sampling seeds, the CSI-M standard deviation is 6 × 10 − 5 6{\times}10^{-5} and the heavy-rain CSIs vary by 2 × 10 − 4 2{\times}10^{-4} (the 16 16 -member probability-matched mean averages out per-sample noise), one to two orders of magnitude below every margin discussed in the main paper.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2609.37487v1 [cs.CV] 27 Sep 2026 Physics-Guided Flow-Map Matching for Precipitation Nowcasting Shunya Nagashima (✉) Affiliation: Neurogica Inc., Tokyo, Japan E-mail shunya.nagashima@neurogica.com Takumi Bannai Affiliation: LTS, Inc., Tokyo, Japan Affiliation: ME-Lab Japan, Inc., Tokyo, Japan Makoto Misaizu Affiliation: Neurogica Inc., Tokyo, Japan E-mail shunya.nagashima@neurogica.com Affiliation: Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan Keisuke Maeda Affiliation: Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan Takahiro Ogawa Affiliation: Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan Miki Haseyama Affiliation: Hokkaido University, Sapporo, Japan Abstract Precipitation nowcasting, generating future radar fields from past observations, is critical for flood warning and disaster response. It is also a demanding benchmark for spatiotemporal generative modeling, with chaotic dynamics, heavy-tailed intensities, and rare high-intensity structures that matter most. Deterministic models minimize a pixel loss and are driven toward the conditional mean, which blurs exactly those structures, while generative models that add a stochastic residual on top of a deterministic backbone inherit the same blur. We propose Physics-Guided Flow-Map Matching (PG-FMM), a conditional flow-map model that decouples predictable advection from uncertain small-scale detail. A frozen Lagrangian advection prior transports the radar field and supplies an explicit motion forecast, and a flow-map generative head, conditioned on the past frames and the prior rollout rather than summed onto it, produces sharp stochastic detail in four sampling steps. The prior serves only as guidance, so the head replaces blurred structure instead of inheriting it. Extensive experiments on four radar benchmarks show that PG-FMM outperforms state-of-the-art methods on 18 18 of 24 24 metrics, with the largest gains at heavy-rain thresholds, where the critical success index improves by up to 58.9 % 58.9\% . The project page can be found at https://neurogica.github.io/PG-FMM . Keywords: Flow matching Generative models Spatio-temporal modeling Video prediction Precipitation nowcasting 1 Introduction Figure 1 : Three families of precipitation nowcasters: (1) deterministic models blur high-intensity cells; (2) purely generative models can drift off the observed storm track; (3) our physics-guided design conditions a flow-map head on a frozen advection prior, keeping forecasts sharp and on track. Precipitation nowcasting generates the next one to two hours of high-resolution reflectivity fields from a short history of radar frames. It is conditional video prediction in a demanding regime, as the dynamics are chaotic, the intensity distribution is heavy-tailed, and forecast value is concentrated in rare high-intensity structures. Nowcasts underpin flood early warning, disaster response, water management, and the safe operation of transport and energy infrastructure [ 2 , 43 , 60 ] , and their importance grows as a warming climate intensifies short-duration convective rainfall extremes and the flash flooding they cause [ 12 ] ; the short lead time of a nowcast often separates an effective response from a costly one. A useful nowcast must therefore forecast where and how strongly convective cells will develop, not merely whether it will rain. This high-intensity regime is also the hardest, because small-scale convective growth and decay are only partly predictable. Deterministic video predictors minimize a per-pixel regression loss and are therefore driven toward the conditional mean of the future, so their forecasts blur [ 46 , 47 , 54 , 14 , 16 ] . The blur erases sharp, high-intensity cores, and detection skill at the heaviest thresholds decays toward zero as the lead time grows. This failure mode is shared even by strong recent predictors such as PhyDNet [ 26 ] and AlphaPre [ 28 ] , because a mean-seeking objective smooths extremes regardless of the backbone. A faithful nowcaster must therefore be generative, sampling sharp and plausible fields rather than averaging them. Existing generative nowcasters address sharpness but leave two gaps. Many recent diffusion-based methods anchor the forecast on a deterministic backbone, refining it or adding a stochastic residual to it [ 18 , 59 ] ; because that backbone is trained with a pixel loss, it carries conditional-mean blur, which the anchored forecast inherits at long lead times. Purely generative models, including GAN- and flow-based nowcasters [ 43 , 39 ] , avoid the anchor but discard the predictable part of the dynamics, namely the advective motion that a simple physical model already captures well, and must relearn it from data, which can drift the forecast off the observed storm track. These gaps motivate a design that retains the motion skill of a physical model while letting a generative model render the unpredictable detail, without either contaminating the other. Figure 1 contrasts deterministic, purely generative, and our physics-guided designs. In this paper we propose Physics-Guided Flow-Map Matching (PG-FMM), a generative nowcaster that guides a flow-map generative head with a frozen physical motion model. A lightweight Lagrangian advection prior is pre-trained once and then frozen; it rolls the observed field forward through a learned velocity and source term and supplies an explicit motion forecast. A flow-map generative head then produces the future sequence conditioned on both the history and this prior rollout. A central design choice is that the prior enters as a conditioning signal rather than as an additive residual, so the head can replace the prior’s blurred structure with sharper detail while still exploiting its motion skill, and the physical rollout keeps the convection on a plausible trajectory. Here physics-guided means that the prior’s rollout is a discretized advection equation in which only the coefficient fields are learned ( Sec. 4.2 ). Casting the generator as a two-time flow map rather than an instantaneous velocity field lets it produce a forecast in a few network evaluations, in line with recent flow-map and consistency models [ 6 , 48 ] . This separation of predictable motion from stochastic detail follows the decoupling logic proposed in [ 34 ] . Across four standard radar benchmarks and six metrics each, PG-FMM outperforms the state-of-the-art AlphaPre [ 28 ] on 18 18 of the 24 24 metrics, and the margins are largest precisely at the heavy-rain thresholds where mean-seeking methods fail. Code and pretrained checkpoints are publicly available. 1 1 1 https://github.com/Neurogica/PG-FMM The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows. ∙ \bullet We propose PG-FMM, which guides a generative flow-map head with a frozen Lagrangian advection prior used as conditioning rather than an additive residual, so conditional-mean blur is never inherited additively. ∙ \bullet We introduce, to our knowledge, the first flow-map-matching formulation for precipitation nowcasting, coupling a learned semi-Lagrangian advection prior with a two-time transport head whose few-step sampling makes the inference-time ensemble affordable. ∙ \bullet We show on the SEVIR, MeteoNet, Shanghai, and CIKM benchmarks that PG-FMM surpasses AlphaPre on 18 18 of 24 24 metrics, with the largest gains at the heavy-rain thresholds, and we isolate the prior’s contribution with controlled ablations, which show that its benefit stems from the physics content rather than from conditioning alone. 2 Related Work 2.1 Video Prediction and Precipitation Nowcasting Radar nowcasting is a conditional video-prediction problem, and the two literatures have co-evolved since ConvLSTM [ 46 ] , which was introduced for nowcasting and became a standard video-prediction baseline [ 36 , 33 ] . Deterministic sequence predictors developed on video transfer directly to radar, including trajectory-aware recurrence (TrajGRU [ 47 ] , the PredRNN family [ 54 , 53 , 55 ] , MotionRNN [ 56 ] ), efficient convolutional designs (SimVP [ 14 ] , MAU [ 8 ] ), and transformer and operator backbones (Earthformer [ 16 ] , Rainformer [ 4 ] ); physically structured predictors such as PhyDNet [ 26 ] and the recent amplitude–phase model AlphaPre [ 28 ] , the strongest deterministic predictor on the benchmarks we use, continue this line, and surveys cover both the video and the weather perspective [ 2 , 45 ] . Because a squared- or absolute-error objective is minimized by the conditional mean, all of these models tend to blur, and the blur is most damaging at high reflectivity where sharp convective cells are smoothed away. Stochastic video generation addresses the blur by sampling futures rather than averaging them, as in video-diffusion predictors such as MCVD [ 52 ] and STRPM [ 7 ] . On radar, DGMR [ 43 ] uses a conditional GAN, and NowcastNet [ 60 ] couples a deterministic evolution operator with a generative network. Diffusion and latent-diffusion models have since become dominant. PreDiff [ 15 ] and LDCast [ 27 ] perform latent diffusion, CasCast [ 18 ] cascades a deterministic prediction with a latent diffusion refiner, and DiffCast [ 59 ] adds a stochastic residual on top of an arbitrary deterministic backbone. We refer to the latter recipe as a residual anchor: the forecast is a deterministic prediction plus a generated residual. Because the deterministic part is trained with a pixel loss, it carries conditional-mean blur that the sum cannot remove, particularly at long lead times. Diffusion models for the broader weather-forecasting problem [ 40 , 50 , 35 ] share the same generative motivation at coarser scales. 2.2 Flow Matching and Flow Maps Continuous-time generative models have matured rapidly, and recent surveys [ 58 , 30 ] cover the progression from score-based diffusion [ 19 , 49 , 21 ] to simulation-free transport. Flow Matching [ 29 ] , Rectified Flow [ 32 ] , and Stochastic Interpolants [ 1 ] regress an instantaneous velocity field whose probability-flow ODE must be integrated with many steps at sampling time. Flow-Map Matching [ 6 ] instead learns the finite-time flow map (the two-time transport operator), so that a sample is produced in a few network evaluations, or even one; Consistency Models [ 48 ] , Consistency Trajectory Models [ 22 ] , and Shortcut Models [ 13 ] reach the same few-step regime through self-consistency, trajectory matching, and step-size conditioning, and distillation offers a complementary route [ 44 ] ; data-to-data diffusion bridges [ 31 , 61 ] are related transport formulations. In nowcasting, FlowCast [ 39 ] applies conditional flow matching in a latent space. We adopt a flow-map head because its few-step sampling makes a multi-member inference ensemble affordable, which is otherwise prohibitive for long diffusion chains. 2.3 Physics-Informed and Lagrangian Forecasting Physics-informed machine learning injects physical knowledge into data-driven models through soft PDE-residual penalties, structured operators, or explicit dynamics, and is reviewed comprehensively by Karniadakis et al . [ 20 , 42 ] . In precipitation nowcasting, a long operational tradition extrapolates the radar field along estimated motion, as in the optical-flow libraries PySTEPS [ 41 ] and rainymotion [ 3 ] ; such Lagrangian advection is accurate for short horizons but cannot represent growth or decay. Learning-based work reintroduces the missing source term while keeping the motion explicit: NowcastNet [ 60 ] learns a neural evolution operator with an additive intensity update, PhyDNet [ 26 ] disentangles physical dynamics from residual factors in a latent space, and the differentiable Lagrangian network LUPIN [ 38 ] separates advection from an advection-free growth/decay branch. Beyond nowcasting, large data-driven weather models [ 37 , 5 , 24 , 23 ] extend physically informed architectures to global forecasting. Our prior follows the explicit warp-and-source route but keeps the physics module lightweight and, after a short pre-training stage, frozen, so that it supplies motion skill as a conditioning signal, not a constraint on the generative head. 3 Preliminaries 3.1 Problem Setting We address radar precipitation nowcasting. A model observes a history of T in T_{\mathrm{in}} past radar frames and predicts the next T out T_{\mathrm{out}} frames, where each frame is a single-channel reflectivity field R ∈ ℝ H × W R\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} on a spatial grid of size H × W H\times W normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . We write the observed history as R 1 : T in R_{1:T_{\mathrm{in}}} and the prediction target as x 0 = R T in + 1 : T in + T out ∈ ℝ T out × H × W , x_{0}=R_{T_{\mathrm{in}}+1:\,T_{\mathrm{in}}+T_{\mathrm{out}}}\in\mathbb{R}^{T_{\mathrm{out}}\times H\times W}, (1) where the T out T_{\mathrm{out}} future frames are stacked along the channel axis for the convolutional networks. The horizon lengths T in , T out T_{\mathrm{in}},T_{\mathrm{out}} , the grid size H × W H\times W , and the per-dataset intensity scale used to recover physical units are dataset-specific and are listed in Sec. 5 . Because convective growth and decay are only partly determined by the recent past, the future is inherently uncertain. We therefore model the conditional distribution p ( x 0 ∣ R 1 : T in ) p(x_{0}\mid R_{1:T_{\mathrm{in}}}) and draw an ensemble of forecasts from it rather than predicting a single field. A useful forecast combines high detection skill at the operational intensity thresholds, especially the heavy-rain thresholds, with low pixel error and sharp structure. We report the Critical Success Index (CSI) per threshold and averaged, the Heidke Skill Score (HSS), SSIM, and MSE, with formal definitions deferred to Sec. 5 ; the primary metrics are the mean CSI and the high-threshold CSI. 3.2 Flow Matching and Flow Maps Continuous-time generative models transport a simple base density to the data distribution along an interpolant between a noise sample x 1 ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and a data sample x 0 x_{0} , x τ = ( 1 − τ ) ​ x 0 + τ ​ x 1 , x_{\tau}=(1-\tau)\,x_{0}+\tau\,x_{1}, (2) where τ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \tau\in[0,1] indexes the path from data ( τ = 0 \tau{=}0 ) to noise ( τ = 1 \tau{=}1 ). Flow-Map Matching instead learns the two-time solution operator of the same ODE. Enforcing this composition consistency during training regularizes the learned operator, and because the map spans a finite time interval a sample is produced in a few jumps rather than many small steps. Our generative head ( Sec. 4 ) instantiates a conditional flow map of this form. 4 Method Figure 2 : Overview of PG-FMM. A frozen Lagrangian advection prior g ϕ g_{\phi} produces an explicit motion forecast, and a flow-map head f θ f_{\theta} , conditioned on the history and the prior rollout, maps noise to the future sequence in a few transport steps. Stage 1 is pre-trained and frozen, Stage 2 is trained with the flow-map objective, and PMM denotes the probability-matched mean over K K samples. The prior is never added to the output. 4.1 Overview PG-FMM forecasts precipitation by separating the predictable advective motion of the radar field from the uncertain small-scale detail, so that neither part contaminates the other. The model has two modules ( Fig. 2 ): a frozen Lagrangian advection prior g ϕ g_{\phi} ( Sec. 4.2 ) that turns the observed history into an explicit motion forecast, and a flow-map generative head f θ f_{\theta} ( Sec. 4.3 ) that, conditioned on the history and the prior rollout, samples the future sequence. At inference we aggregate a small ensemble with a probability-matched mean ( Sec. 4.4 ). The prior is used only as conditioning and is never added to the output, unlike residual-anchor nowcasters [ 18 , 59 ] , whose pixel-loss backbone carries its conditional-mean blur into the anchored forecast ( Sec. 2 ). Passing the physical forecast as a conditioning signal instead lets the generative head replace the prior’s blurred structure with sharp detail while still exploiting its motion skill. The decoupling does not depend on the particular modules, as any per-step motion model and any conditional generative head could be substituted. Ours pairs a learned warp-and-source prior with a flow-map head whose few-step sampling keeps the ensemble affordable. 4.2 Lagrangian Advection Prior Precipitation evolves partly through predictable transport and partly through stochastic growth and decay, and a lightweight physical model can already account for the first part. The prior captures this predictable motion explicitly, so the generative head models only the residual uncertainty rather than relearning bulk advection from scratch. The prior is implemented as a U-Net g ϕ g_{\phi} that ingests the stacked history R 1 : T in R_{1:T_{\mathrm{in}}} and emits, for each future step t t , a dense velocity field v t ∈ ℝ 2 × H × W v_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{2\times H\times W} and a scalar source/sink field s t ∈ ℝ H × W s_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W} . The physics prior is best on every metric except SSIM, followed by the learned deterministic prior, and classical advection trails even the no-prior variant on every detection metric. The content of the prior is therefore what matters: a poor prior is worse than no prior at all, so the gains cannot be explained by conditioning alone. The one exception, SSIM, rewards smoother output, as the Prior only row below shows most clearly. The full model in Tab. 1 uses a longer schedule, hence its slightly higher numbers; per-lead-time curves in the supplementary material show that the physics prior’s margin emerges at long lead times. The generative head is likewise necessary. The frozen prior alone (Prior only in Tab. 2 ) is already a strong deterministic baseline, yet it trails the full model on every skill metric; its best-in-table SSIM reflects smoothness, and the head adds the sharpness and probabilistic skill (CRPS). Together, these ablations justify the motion–generative decoupling. The supplementary material reports further studies. Composition consistency ( Eq. 8 ) appears to improve fidelity and stability rather than detection skill, so we keep it enabled. A fusion ablation indicates that conditioning, unlike additive residual fusion, is robust to the quality of the prior. Structural metrics suggest that the heavy-rain gain reflects recovered heavy rain rather than inflated area, and a matched-ensemble comparison with a reproduced generative baseline indicates that the margin persists. 6 Conclusion We addressed radar precipitation nowcasting in the high-intensity regime, where existing models blur the strongest convective cells. PG-FMM decouples predictable advection from uncertain small-scale detail and conditions a flow-map head on a frozen physical prior rather than summing a residual onto it, so no conditional-mean blur is additively inherited. Under a unified protocol over four radar benchmarks, PG-FMM surpassed the state-of-the-art AlphaPre on 18 18 of 24 24 metrics, with the largest margins at the heavy-rain thresholds where mean-seeking methods fail, and controlled ablations isolated the contributions of the prior and the head.
